{"rule":"Return this JSON object with the rule field unchanged and, in the text field, the passage of about 250 words that comes immediately AFTER the current text in the same story.","text":"Across the street, beneath the striped awning of the closed bakery, stood a man with one hand raised against the rain.

Mara knew the shape of his shoulders before she knew his face. She knew the slight tilt of his head, as if he were listening for a train that had already passed.

Her brother looked older, of course. His hair had gone gray at the temples, and a pale scar crossed his chin. But when he lowered his hand, he smiled in exactly the way she remembered: crookedly, like an apology he hadn’t decided to make.

She was out the door before she could think better of it.

They met under the awning. For a few seconds neither spoke. Rain hammered the pavement between them, and a bus sighed past, spraying water along the curb.

“You came back,” Mara said.

“I did.”

“You could have called.”

“I did.” He glanced at the phone in her hand. “Years ago. You changed your number.”

The words landed harder than she expected. She had changed it after their mother’s funeral, after the last unanswered voicemail, after telling herself that silence was proof he had chosen to leave.

“I thought you were gone,” she said.

“I was.” His smile faded. “Then I wasn’t. I didn’t know how to come home.”

Mara looked past him toward the station. “Why the suitcase?”

“Because I didn’t bring anything else.”

He held out a small envelope, softened at the edges by rain. Her name was written across it in their mother’s careful handwriting.

Mara took it, but didn’t open it.

“Did you know what was inside?” she asked.

“No,” he said. “I was hoping you would.”

For the first time, she noticed his hands were shaking. She reached for the envelope with both of hers, and together they turned toward the lighted station."}
